To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) “depression”, diabetes and AD are associated with hypercorticisolaemia and insulin resistance, 2) “depression” preceding PD is not associated with hypercoticisolaemia and 3) “depression associated with diabetes and AD might be a subtype of “depression”, which can be differentiated by clinical, biochemical and molecular markers.

(1) “depression” in a subgroup of depressed subjects with hypercortisolism is associated with insulin resistance and diabetes type II; (2) this subgroup of “depressed” patients is also at risk for developing Alzheimer’s disease; and (3) the association between “depression” (preceding PD in up to 50% of such patients) and diabetes type II is less strong than that between depression and Alzheimer’s disease.
“depression” as a risk factor for AD and PD is associated with disturbances of HPA axis and chronic hypercortisolism.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question, whether the subgroup of “depressed” patients with disturbances of the stress axis, hypercortisolemia and insulin resistance is at risk for AD and whether “depression”, which is not associated to disturbances of the HPC axis is at risk for PD.

the elucidation of the etiology of “depression”, which is associated with hypercorticolaemia and insulin resistance, and which is the subgroup of patients at risk for diabetes type II, Alzheimer’s disease, and Parkinson’s disease.
the question of whether there is a subgroup of “patients with depression” which is at risk of AD and/or PD, and whether this subgroup of patients is associated with hypercorticolaemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“depression” as a risk factor for PD and AD, but not for diabetes type II is not associated with chronic stress, hypercortisolemia, insulin resistance and therefore, not with the metabolic syndrome.
depression is a risk factor for AD and PD, but not for PD.
“depression” as a risk factor for PD, AD and diabetes type II is not supported by the current evidence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

depression associated with AD and diabetes type II might be a subgroup of “pure” depression, which is associated with hypercorticolaemia and hyperinsulinemia, whereas depression associated with PD might be a different subtype of “pure” “depression” which is not associated or even associated with hypocortisolaemia.
“depression” as a risk factor for AD and PD is associated with hypercorticisolaemia, which is not the case for PD and AD.
“depression” might be a risk factor for AD and PD, and that the subgroup associated with diabetes type II is at higher risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is ample evidence that “depression” as a subgroup is associated with hypercorticolaemia and insulin resistance, which is of etiopathological importance for the development of AD, whereas there is only weak association between PD and insulin resistance.
“depression” may be associated with different pathophysiology and that this may lead to a different clinical course of the disease and different response to treatment.
there is a need to further explore the association between depression and diabetes type II, Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
